entities.summary:
Hugh of Lincoln, also known as Hugh of Avalon, was a Burgundian-born Carthusian monk, bishop of Lincoln in the Kingdom of England, and Catholic saint. Born in the early 12th century, little is known of his early life. He was ordained as a priest and became the bishop of Lincoln in 1192, a position he held until his death on November 24, 1200. During his tenure, he oversaw the construction of several churches and monasteries, including the Church of the Holy Trinity in Lincoln.

Hugh of Lincoln was a prominent figure in the Catholic Church and was respected for his piety and wisdom. He was known for his role in the translation of the Bible into English and his efforts to promote education and literacy in England. He was also a strong advocate for the rights of the poor and the marginalized.

Despite his significant contributions to the Catholic Church, Hugh of Lincoln's legacy is not as well-known as that of some of his contemporaries. Nevertheless, his feast day is still celebrated by Catholics around the world on November 16, and his legacy continues to inspire those who seek to follow in his footsteps.

In 2000, the Church of England recognized Hugh of Lincoln as a saint, and his feast day is now also celebrated by Anglicans on November 17. His example serves as a reminder of the importance of faith, compassion, and service to others.

Throughout his life, Hugh of Lincoln remained committed to his faith and his community. He worked tirelessly to promote the values of the Catholic Church and to serve the needs of those around him. His legacy continues to inspire people around the world to live out their faith in practical and meaningful ways.
